plan.title: Recurring Billing Plan 2/2 — Schedules, generation, payment links, editor, cash forecast
plan.goal: Turn the schedules that Plan 1 stores into money: Ledgerline issues each recurring invoice on time and never twice, gives every invoice a card-payment link that marks it paid, lets the owner set up a schedule from the invoice editor on desktop and phone, and shows the next 90 days of expected cash on the dashboard.
plan.architecture: A pure recurrence engine computes occurrences in the schedule's timezone and is the only place calendar rules live. An hourly BullMQ job materialises due invoices behind a database unique index, so a second worker or a retry is a no-op. Payments go out through the existing Tollgate adapter and come back through one signed webhook that records the payment and emits invoice.paid. The web side adds the recurrence panel to the invoice editor and a forecast card to the dashboard, both on TanStack Query.
plan.techStack: Node 22, Express 5, Knex on PostgreSQL 16, BullMQ on Redis 7, date-fns-tz, zod, React 19 + Vite + TanStack Query v5 in web/, Vitest on both sides, Docker Compose.
plan.spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-14-recurring-billing-design.md, sections "Recurrence rules", "Generation and idempotency", "Payment links and webhooks", "Editor and mobile UI" and "Cash forecast".

constraints: Work on feature/ll-87-recurring-billing; every commit carries the Refs LL-87 trailer as its second -m.
Docker only: migrations and tests run through docker exec ledgerline_api ... and docker exec ledgerline_web ...; never run Node on the host.

Server: every route declares a zod schema through validate(); every query filters by account_id from req.auth.accountId; no console.*; outbound HTTP only through the undici client in server/src/lib/http.js; errors are AppError(code, status) with a stable upper-snake code.
Web: design tokens from web/src/styles/tokens.css, the shared Sheet recipe for every drawer, npm run lint:fix before each commit, and a browser check at 360 px and 1280 px for UI tasks.

Money is integer cents with the account currency alongside, formatted only at render time by formatMoney(cents, currency); dates travel as ISO strings (yyyy-MM-dd for calendar dates) and timezone conversion goes through date-fns-tz only.
Before a task is done: its tests pass in Docker, the touched side's full suite passes, and npm run lint:fix leaves no diff.

decisions.text: Plan 1's schedules.timezone always holds a valid IANA name; rows imported by its migration script were never re-validated.

With skip_weekends on, a Saturday or Sunday moves back to Friday rather than forward to Monday. Friday is implemented because it never pushes an invoice into the next month. Product-confirm before release.
Generated invoices (A) stay as drafts for the owner to review and send (implemented), or (B) go out to the customer automatically at 06:00 local. Product-confirm before release.
options: A: stay as drafts for the owner (implemented)

decisions.text: When a paused schedule is resumed, does it generate the periods it missed while paused, or start from the next future period? The 7-day lookback currently backfills up to a week.
options: Start from the next future period

decisions.text: Tollgate presumably retries a failed webhook delivery for up to 72 hours; the webhook_events primary key ignores every repeat either way.
Can a bookkeeper pause and resume a schedule without being able to edit it? Today pausing is a PUT and needs schedules:write, which only owners hold.

overview.text: Goal. Turn the schedules that plan one stores into money. Ledgerline issues each recurring invoice on time and never twice, gives every invoice a card payment link that marks it paid, lets the owner set up a schedule from the invoice editor on desktop and phone, and shows the next ninety days of expected cash on the dashboard.

Architecture. A pure recurrence engine computes occurrences in the schedule timezone and is the only place calendar rules live. An hourly Bull M Q job creates due invoices behind a database unique index, so a second worker or a retry changes nothing. Payments return through one signed Tollgate webhook that records the payment and emits invoice paid. The web side adds the editor panel and a dashboard forecast card.

Tech stack. Node twenty two, Express five, Knex on Postgres sixteen, and Bull M Q on Redis seven on the server, with date f n s t z for timezones and zod for validation. The web side uses React nineteen, Vite and TanStack Query version five. Vitest tests both sides, and Docker Compose runs everything.

Task map. Five tasks joined by five links. The recurrence engine feeds invoice generation, the recurrence panel and the cash forecast, each with next occurrences. Invoice generation feeds the cash forecast with the invoice schedule I D column. Payment links feed the cash forecast with the invoice paid event, which drops its cache. The wrap up then verifies everything end to end.

decisions.text: Assumption, for the recurrence engine. Every plan one schedule holds a valid I A N A timezone name. Plan one validates on write, but rows imported by its migration script were never validated again, so one bad imported value would break the occurrence dates of that schedule.

Confirm, for the recurrence engine. With skip weekends on, a Saturday or Sunday moves back to Friday rather than forward to Monday. Friday is implemented because it never pushes an invoice into the next month. Product confirm before release. Options: back to Friday, as implemented, or forward to Monday.

Confirm, for invoice generation. Option A: generated invoices stay as drafts for the owner to review and send, which is implemented. Option B: they go out to the customer automatically at six in the morning, local time. Product confirm before release which of the two ships.

Open question, for invoice generation. When a paused schedule is resumed, does it generate the periods it missed while paused, or start from the next future period? The seven day lookback currently backfills up to a week. Options: generate the missed periods, or start from the next future period.

Assumption, for payment links. Tollgate presumably retries a failed webhook delivery for up to seventy two hours. The design does not depend on the exact window: the webhook events primary key ignores any repeat of the same event, whether it is a retry or a captured body replayed within five minutes.

Open question, for the recurrence panel. Can a bookkeeper pause and resume a schedule without being able to edit it? Today pausing is a put request to the schedule route, so it needs the schedules write permission, which only owners hold. This is a yes or no question for product.

sections.title: Context
sections.summary: Plan 2 of 2 for recurring billing. Plan 1 delivered the schedules table, an empty recurrence panel shell in the invoice editor behind the recurring_billing flag, and a Tollgate adapter smoke-tested against the sandbox; this plan makes all three do real work. The developer owns three prerequisites: sandbox keys, a manually registered webhook secret, and a per-environment permission grant.

consumes: recurrence panel shell in the invoice editor, behind the recurring_billing flag (Plan 1)

risks: Manual step: register https://<tunnel-host>/api/webhooks/tollgate for checkout.completed in the Tollgate dashboard, copy the signing secret into TOLLGATE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, and repeat for staging and production. Without it every webhook answers 400 and no invoice is ever marked paid by card.

Manual step: run npm run perms:grant -- recurring-billing once per environment after Task 4 lands (LL-61). Without the grant every new route 403s for real accounts while the tests stay green, because the test harness grants all permissions.

narration.text: Context. This is plan two of two for recurring billing. Plan one delivered the schedules table, an empty recurrence panel in the invoice editor behind a feature flag, and a Tollgate payment adapter tested against its sandbox. This plan makes all three do real work. The developer owns three prerequisites: sandbox keys, a webhook secret, and a permission grant.

Consumes three things from plan one: the schedules table, the empty recurrence panel shell, and the Tollgate adapter. It also needs three settings in the development environment file: the Tollgate A P I key, the Tollgate account I D, and the webhook signing secret. The preamble itself produces nothing; the tasks that follow pick up everything it names.

Two manual steps. Register the webhook in the Tollgate dashboard and copy its signing secret for every environment; without it every webhook answers four hundred and no invoice is marked paid by card. And run the recurring billing permission grant once per environment after task four; without it every new route answers four oh three for real accounts while the tests stay green.

sections.title: Task 1: Recurrence engine
sections.summary: A pure function that turns a schedule row into its next occurrences, the only place calendar rules live. It clamps anchor days to short months, can move weekend dates back to Friday, honours an end date or a count, and issues each occurrence at 06:00 in the schedule's timezone, steady across daylight-saving changes.

produces: nextOccurrences(schedule, from, count) returning { nominalOn, issueOn, issueAt }[]

risks: DST gotcha: adding 24 hours to a UTC instant drifts by an hour twice a year, so the engine derives the local date first and converts 06:00 local wall time once, at the end.

blocks.summary: Three Vitest cases against a monthly Europe/Lisbon schedule: an anchor of 31 clamps to the last day of shorter months, a Saturday moves back to Friday when skip_weekends is on, and the issue instant stays at 06:00 local on both sides of the October DST change.
behaviors: clamps an anchor of 31 to the last day of shorter months
moves weekend dates back to Friday when skip_weekends is on
issues at 06:00 local time on both sides of a DST change

blocks.summary: Calendar helpers do date arithmetic on yyyy-MM-dd strings through Date.UTC, so the host timezone never leaks in. candidateAt steps weekly schedules from the anchor weekday and the others by whole months, clamping the anchor to the month length. nextOccurrences stops at max_count or ends_on, applies the weekend shift, skips dates before today in the schedule's timezone, and converts 06:00 local to a UTC instant once.

sections.executorDetail:
- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests**

- [ ] **Step 2: Implement the engine**

Calendar arithmetic runs on `yyyy-MM-dd` strings through `Date.UTC`, so the host timezone never leaks in. DST gotcha: adding 24 hours to a UTC instant drifts by an hour twice a year, so the engine derives the local date first and converts 06:00 local wall time once, at the end. Assume Plan 1's `schedules.timezone` always holds a valid IANA name; rows imported by its migration script were never re-validated.

Product-confirm before release that `skip_weekends` moves a Saturday or Sunday back to Friday rather than forward to Monday; Friday is implemented because it never pushes an invoice into the next month.

- [ ] **Step 3: Run the tests and commit**

```bash
docker exec ledgerline_api npx vitest run test/billing/recurrence.test.js
```

```bash
git add server/src/billing/recurrence.js server/test/billing/recurrence.test.js
git commit -m "feat(billing): add the recurrence engine" -m "Refs LL-87"
```

narration.text: Task one, recurrence engine. A pure function turns a schedule row into its next occurrences, and it is the only place calendar rules live. It clamps anchor days to short months, can move weekend dates back to Friday, honours an end date or a count, and issues every occurrence at six in the morning, local time, steady across daylight saving changes.

Consumes seven columns of the plan one schedules table: frequency, anchor day, starts on, ends on, maximum count, skip weekends and timezone. Produces next occurrences, which takes a schedule, a starting instant and a count, and returns a list of occurrences, each with a nominal date, an issue date and an issue instant in U T C.

Two decisions. An assumption: every schedule holds a valid I A N A timezone name, even rows imported by the plan one migration script, which were never validated again. And a confirm: weekend dates move back to Friday, as implemented, or forward to Monday; Friday never pushes an invoice into the next month.

Risk, the daylight saving gotcha. Adding twenty four hours to a U T C instant drifts by an hour twice a year. The engine avoids it by doing all calendar arithmetic on plain date strings, deriving the local date first, and converting six in the morning local time to an instant only once, at the very end.

Code block one, recurrence dot test dot j s. Three Vitest cases against a monthly Lisbon schedule. An anchor of thirty one clamps to the last day of shorter months, such as February twenty eighth. A Saturday moves back to Friday when skip weekends is on. And the issue time stays at six local on both sides of a daylight saving change.

Code block two, recurrence dot j s. Small helpers do calendar arithmetic on date strings through U T C, so the host timezone never leaks in. Weekly schedules step seven days from the anchor weekday; the others step whole months and clamp the anchor to the month length. The loop stops at the count or end date, applies the weekend shift, and skips dates already past.

sections.title: Task 2: Invoice generation job
sections.summary: An hourly job that turns every due occurrence of every active schedule into a draft invoice copied from the schedule's template. A unique index on schedule and period makes it idempotent, so two racing workers or a retry produce exactly one invoice, and the number is allocated only after the insert wins so a losing racer never burns one.

changes.role: migration adding schedule_id, period_key and their unique index

risks: Race: two workers that pick up the same hourly tick both reach the insert; the invoices_schedule_period_unique index lets PostgreSQL accept one row and the other insert becomes a no-op.

blocks.summary: Vitest cases against a seeded monthly schedule starting 2026-11-01: the first period becomes a draft carrying the template's two lines, two concurrent calls for the same period create one invoice, and a repeated call leaves the account's next invoice number at 2.
behaviors: copies the template lines into a draft for the period
creates one invoice when two workers race for the same period
does not burn an invoice number when the period already exists

blocks.summary: generateForPeriod runs in one transaction: it loads the template scoped to the account, inserts the draft with an ignored conflict on schedule and period, and returns created false when the insert lost. Only the winner copies the template lines and then allocates the invoice number, so a lost race never consumes one.

sections.executorDetail:
- [ ] **Step 1: Migration and failing tests**

The migration adds `invoices.schedule_id` (nullable, references `schedules.id`, `ON DELETE SET NULL`) and `invoices.period_key` (`varchar(10)`, the occurrence's `nominalOn`), with the unique index `invoices_schedule_period_unique` on the pair. That index is the guard against the double-generation race: two workers that pick up the same hourly tick both reach the insert, PostgreSQL lets one row through, and the other insert becomes a no-op.

- [ ] **Step 2: Implement generation and register the job**

The invoice number is allocated only after the insert wins, so a losing racer never consumes one.

`generateDueInvoices(db, now)` in the same file loops over active schedules, takes `nextOccurrences(schedule, now - 7 days, 10)` whose `issueAt` has passed, and calls `generateForPeriod` for each. Register `generate-due-invoices` in `server/src/jobs/index.js` with `{ pattern: '5 * * * *' }`. Product-confirm before release, option A or B: generated invoices (A) stay as drafts for the owner to review and send (implemented), or (B) go out to the customer automatically at 06:00 local. Open question: when a paused schedule is resumed, does it generate the periods it missed while paused, or start from the next future period? The 7-day lookback currently backfills up to a week.

- [ ] **Step 3: Run the tests and commit**

```bash
docker exec ledgerline_api npx knex migrate:latest
docker exec ledgerline_api npx vitest run test/billing
```

```bash
git add server/migrations/20261008090000_invoice_schedule_period.js server/src/billing/generate.js server/src/jobs/index.js server/test/billing/generate.test.js
git commit -m "feat(billing): generate due invoices hourly, once per period" -m "Refs LL-87"
```

narration.text: Task two, invoice generation job. An hourly job turns every due occurrence of every active schedule into a draft invoice copied from the schedule template. A unique index on schedule and period makes it idempotent, so two racing workers or a retry produce exactly one invoice, and the number is allocated only after the insert wins.

Consumes next occurrences from task one and the existing allocate invoice number function. Produces two new invoice columns, schedule I D and period key, with a unique index over the pair; generate for period, which turns one occurrence into a draft; and the hourly Bull M Q job named generate due invoices, which runs five minutes past every hour.

Two decisions. A confirm with options A and B: generated invoices stay as drafts for the owner to send, as implemented, or go out automatically at six in the morning local time. And an open question: when a paused schedule resumes, does it generate the periods it missed, or start from the next future period?

Risk, the double generation race. Two workers that pick up the same hourly tick both reach the insert. The unique index on schedule and period lets Postgres accept exactly one row, and the other insert becomes a no op. The index, not any check in memory, is what keeps an invoice from being issued twice.

Code block one, generate dot test dot j s. Three Vitest cases against a seeded monthly schedule. The first period becomes a draft carrying both template lines. Two concurrent calls for the same period create exactly one invoice. And calling twice for a period that already exists leaves the account next invoice number at two, so no number is burned.

Code block two, generate dot j s. Generate for period runs in one transaction. It loads the template inside the account, inserts the draft while ignoring a conflict on schedule and period, and returns not created when the insert lost. Only the winner copies the template lines and then allocates the invoice number, so a lost race never consumes one.

sections.title: Task 3: Payment links and the Tollgate webhook
sections.summary: Every invoice gets a reusable Tollgate checkout link, and Tollgate's signed webhook records the card payment and emits invoice.paid. The webhook checks an HMAC signature with a five-minute tolerance and records each event id once, so retries and replays never pay an invoice twice.

changes.role: app wiring: webhook mounted before express.json()

consumes: existing recordPayment(trx, { invoiceId, amountCents, method, reference })

blocks.summary: Supertest cases that sign bodies with the signTollgateBody helper against a seeded payment link: a completed checkout marks the invoice paid, the same event replayed records one payment, and a correctly signed body older than five minutes is rejected with 400 WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_INVALID.
behaviors: marks the invoice paid on checkout.completed
records the payment once when the same event is replayed
rejects a correctly signed body older than five minutes

blocks.summary: The route reads the raw JSON body, rejects a bad signature with WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_INVALID (400), and parses only checkout.completed events with zod. In one transaction it records the event id and stops if it was already seen, locks the payment link by session, marks it completed and records the payment. invoice.paid is emitted after commit.

sections.executorDetail:
- [ ] **Step 1: Links, signature check, migration and failing tests**

The migration creates `payment_links` (`account_id`, `invoice_id`, `tollgate_session_id` unique, `url`, `status`, `expires_at`) and `webhook_events` keyed by `event_id`. `createPaymentLink(invoice)` reuses an open link with more than an hour left, else creates a Tollgate session for `balance_cents`; `POST /api/invoices/:id/payment-link` exposes it. `verifyWebhookSignature(rawBody, header, secret)` in `tollgate.js` compares an HMAC-SHA256 of `"<t>.<rawBody>"` with `timingSafeEqual` and rejects a `t` older than 300 seconds.

- [ ] **Step 2: The webhook endpoint**

The `webhook_events` primary key is the replay guard. Tollgate presumably retries a failed delivery for up to 72 hours, and a captured signed body can be resent inside the 300-second window; either way the second insert is ignored and the handler answers 200 without touching the invoice.

Mount it in `server/src/app.js` before `express.json()` so the raw body reaches the signature check.

- [ ] **Step 3: Run the tests and commit**

```bash
docker exec ledgerline_api npx knex migrate:latest
docker exec ledgerline_api npx vitest run test/routes/webhooks-tollgate.test.js
```

```bash
git add server/migrations/20261008091000_payment_links.js server/src/payments server/src/routes/webhooks-tollgate.js server/src/app.js server/test/routes/webhooks-tollgate.test.js
git commit -m "feat(payments): add Tollgate payment links and the signed webhook" -m "Refs LL-87"
```

narration.text: Task three, payment links and the Tollgate webhook. Every invoice gets a reusable Tollgate checkout link, and the signed Tollgate webhook records the card payment and emits invoice paid. The webhook checks an H M A C signature with a five minute tolerance and records each event I D once, so retries and replays never pay an invoice twice.

Consumes the existing create checkout session call and the existing record payment function. Produces create payment link, which reuses an open link with more than an hour left or makes a new one; a post route at slash api slash invoices slash I D slash payment link; the webhook post route at slash api slash webhooks slash tollgate; and the invoice paid event.

One assumption. Tollgate presumably retries a failed delivery for up to seventy two hours. The design does not depend on that window, because the webhook events primary key ignores any repeat of the same event, whether it is a retry or a captured signed body replayed inside the five minute tolerance.

Code block one, webhooks tollgate dot test dot j s. Three Supertest cases that sign bodies with a test helper. A completed checkout marks the invoice paid. The same event delivered twice records exactly one payment. And a correctly signed body older than five minutes is rejected with a four hundred and the signature invalid code.

Code block two, webhooks tollgate dot j s. The route reads the raw body, rejects a bad signature with a four hundred, and accepts only completed checkout events. In one transaction it records the event I D and stops if it was seen before, locks the payment link, marks it completed and records the payment. Invoice paid is emitted only after commit.

sections.executorDetail:
- [ ] **Step 1: Schedule endpoints and hook**

`server/src/routes/schedules.js` validates the body with a `zod` schema mirroring Plan 1's columns (weekly anchors 1–7, an end date and a count mutually exclusive). `GET` and `PUT /api/invoices/:invoiceId/schedule` return `{ schedule, upcoming: nextOccurrences(schedule, new Date(), 3) }`; `PUT` upserts on `template_invoice_id`. `POST /api/schedules/preview` returns `upcoming` for an unsaved draft. Add `schedules:read` (owner, bookkeeper) and `schedules:write` (owner) to `permissions.js`. `useSchedule.js` exports `useSchedule(invoiceId)` (the `GET` plus a `PUT` mutation that refreshes `['schedule', invoiceId]` and `['forecast']`), `usePreview(draft)` and `defaultSchedule()`; `describeSchedule(schedule)` builds the sentence both views show. Open question: can a bookkeeper pause and resume a schedule without being able to edit it? Today pausing is a `PUT` and needs `schedules:write`.

- [ ] **Step 2: The panel at 1280 px**

At 1280 px the editor has line items on the left (about 840 px) and a 360 px sidebar; the panel is the third sidebar card, under "Customer" and "Payment".
- Header row: repeat icon, "Repeat this invoice", an on/off switch right-aligned. Off: a muted line "Send this invoice on a schedule."
- On, top to bottom: a summary sentence on a tinted strip ("Monthly on the 1st, starting Nov 1, 2026, until cancelled"); a full-width segmented control "Weekly | Monthly | Quarterly | Yearly"; "On" select and "Starts" date side by side; an "Ends" radio group ("Never", "On <date>", "After <n> invoices"); a "Move weekend dates to Friday" checkbox.
- "Next 3 invoices": three rows, issue date left and template total right; a weekend-shifted row adds a muted "moved from Sat".
- Footer: "Pause" ghost button left (saved schedules only), "Save schedule" primary right.

`RecurrencePanel` wraps `RecurrenceForm` in the sidebar card with the header switch.

- [ ] **Step 3: The summary at 360 px**

Below 768 px the editor stacks into one column. The recurrence card becomes one tappable 72 px row inside 16 px gutters: repeat icon left; the summary sentence clamped to two lines with a "Next: Mon, Nov 2" chip under it; an "Active" (green) or "Paused" (grey) pill and a chevron on the right. Tapping opens a bottom `Sheet` at 90 % height titled "Repeat this invoice" with the same form in one column and "Save schedule" full width in a sticky footer.

`InvoiceEditor.jsx` renders `RecurrencePanel` at 768 px and up, `ScheduleSummary` below; check both widths in the browser.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run the tests and commit**

```bash
docker exec ledgerline_api npx vitest run test/routes
docker exec ledgerline_web npx vitest run src/invoices
```

```bash
git add server/src/routes/schedules.js server/src/auth/permissions.js web/src/invoices
git commit -m "feat(invoices): add the recurrence panel and the mobile schedule summary" -m "Refs LL-87"
```

narration.text: Task four, recurrence panel and mobile schedule summary. The owner sets up a schedule from the invoice editor: a sidebar panel on desktop, and a tappable summary row that opens a bottom sheet on phones. Both share one form and a live preview of the next three invoices. Behind them, new routes read, save and preview schedules under new read and write permissions.

Consumes next occurrences, the shared sheet component and the empty panel slot plan one left in the editor. Produces get and put routes at slash api slash invoices slash invoice I D slash schedule, a preview route at slash api slash schedules slash preview, the use schedule hook, the describe schedule sentence builder, and the recurrence panel and schedule summary components.

Then it walks up to 60 future occurrences per active schedule and adds the template total in the week of issue date plus payment terms. It returns the weeks and the total in cents.

sections.executorDetail:
- [ ] **Step 1: Forecast service**

Open invoices land in the week of their `due_on`; drafts with a `schedule_id` count as open; future occurrences land in the week of `issueOn + payment_terms_days`. `GET /api/forecast` caches the result per account for an hour and drops the cache on `invoice.paid`.

- [ ] **Step 2: The card at 1280 px**

The dashboard at 1280 px is a grid; the forecast card is about 720 px wide, in the first row beside the existing "Outstanding" card, not full width.
- Header row: "Cash forecast" with a muted "next 90 days" on the left; the total on the right in large tabular figures over a muted "expected".
- Legend: "Open invoices" (solid) and "Scheduled" (lighter tint of the same hue).
- Chart, 200 px tall: thirteen stacked weekly bars, open at the bottom; week-start labels ("Oct 12") under every other bar; hovering a bar shows the week and both amounts.
- Footer: three tiles, "Next 30 days", "31–60 days", "61–90 days".
- Empty state: "No expected income yet." with a "Set up a recurring invoice" link.

`CashForecastCard` queries `['forecast', 90]` and draws the bars as one SVG `<g>` per week holding two `<rect>`s scaled to the busiest week, with a `<title>` for the hover text. Header, legend, tiles and empty state: copy the markup of `web/src/dashboard/OutstandingCard.jsx`. Add the card to `Dashboard.jsx` behind the `recurring_billing` flag; at 360 px it takes the full column and the tiles stack.

- [ ] **Step 3: Run the tests and commit**

```bash
docker exec ledgerline_api npx vitest run test/billing
docker exec ledgerline_web npx vitest run src/dashboard
```

```bash
git add server/src/billing/forecast.js web/src/dashboard
git commit -m "feat(dashboard): add the 90-day cash forecast card" -m "Refs LL-87"
```

sections.title: Verification and hand-over
sections.summary: The closing checks before merge: both suites after a full migration round-trip, lint, and manual checks on the dev stack that a schedule saves at both widths, two workers produce one invoice, a replayed webhook records one payment, and the October DST change keeps the 06:00 issue time. It ends with the staging permission grant and the merge request listing items awaiting product sign-off.
sections.executorDetail:
- Run both full suites in Docker: `docker exec ledgerline_api npx vitest run` and `docker exec ledgerline_web npx vitest run`, after `npx knex migrate:rollback --all` and `migrate:latest` to prove the migrations round-trip.
- Run `npm run lint:fix` at the repository root and review any diff it leaves.
- Open an invoice at 1280 px and at 360 px and save a monthly schedule from each layout; the dashboard forecast shows the new schedule's bars.
- On the dev stack, scale to two workers (`docker compose up -d --scale ledgerline_worker=2`) and check that one weekly schedule starting today yields exactly one invoice after the next tick.
- Pay that invoice through its Tollgate link, then resend the same event from the Tollgate dashboard and check that one payment row exists.
- Set the account timezone to `Europe/Lisbon` and check that the 2026-10-25 DST change leaves the issue time at 06:00 local.
- Run `npm run perms:grant -- recurring-billing` against staging (LL-61) and sign in as a real bookkeeper: the schedule and forecast endpoints answer 200, not 403.
- Push the branch and open the merge request with `glab mr create --target-branch main --title "Recurring billing (LL-87)"`, its description closing LL-87 and listing the items still awaiting product sign-off.

narration.text: Verification and hand over. Both test suites run in Docker after rolling every migration back and forward again, then lint. By hand on the dev stack: save a schedule at both widths, scale to two workers and see exactly one invoice, replay a paid webhook and see one payment, and confirm the October daylight saving change keeps six in the morning. Then grant staging permissions and open the merge request.
